"Inanimate" means not alive. When you describe something as inanimate, you are saying it has no life — no heartbeat, no breath, no ability to grow, feel, or reproduce on its own. It simply exists as matter.

A rock is inanimate. A chair is inanimate. A glass of water, a coin, a building, a cloud — all inanimate. They exist in the world, but they do not live.

The direct opposite of "inanimate" is animate. Animate things are alive — humans and animals clearly qualify, and so do plants. Everything else — the physical, non-living world of objects and materials — is inanimate.

A simple way to think about it: if something has never been alive and cannot become alive on its own, it is inanimate.
The cases that might confuse you

Robots and machines: A robot can walk, speak, and appear to "think." But it is still inanimate — it has no biology, no cells, no life of its own. It moves only because a human engineered it to do so.

Fire: Fire grows, spreads, and consumes fuel, so it can seem alive. But fire is a chemical reaction, not a living organism. It is inanimate.

Plants: This is where many people stumble. Plants are actually alive — they grow, reproduce, and respond to light and water. So plants are not inanimate. They are animate, even though they cannot move or speak.

A dead animal: An animal that has died was once animate. After death, it becomes inanimate — life has left it. So "inanimate" can also describe something that was alive but no longer is.

In everyday language, people sometimes use "inanimate" more loosely to describe a person or performance that seems dull, spiritless, or without energy — as though the life has been drained from them. For example: "His inanimate expression made it clear he wasn't interested." This usage borrows from the core idea of "lifeless" but applies it to spirit and emotion rather than biology. It is less common and more literary in tone.
How it is used in sentences

• "The museum displayed inanimate artifacts — pottery, coins, and ancient tools."
  • "A sculptor's art is to bring beauty out of an inanimate block of stone."
  • "Unlike living creatures, inanimate objects cannot feel pain or fear."
  • "The children's story imagined a world where inanimate things — chairs, clocks, and teapots — could talk."

"Inanimate" is an adjective that describes anything with no life in it. The non-living, physical world around you — furniture, rocks, machines, water, soil — is made up of inanimate things, and the word is most commonly paired with the noun "object," as in inanimate object, to draw a clean line between the living and the non-living.
